steps.caption: White to move. Black's last move put a knight on b4, next to the bishop on f5. Before you play anything, count the attackers and defenders of the pawn on c2.

claims.statement: Black has two attackers on c2 (the knight on b4 and the bishop on f5).
White has one defender of c2 (the queen).

steps.chapter: Count first: the pawn on c2

steps.text: **Two against one.** The knight and the bishop both aim at c2, and only the queen guards it. If the pawn leaves c2, the knight can land there with check and attack the rook on a1 as well. The natural-looking reply, a pawn to c3 that hits the knight, is the very move that opens c2. In our online data (4,752,291 games) White played it in 74 of the 862 games in which Black played ...Nb4 here [V].

steps.caption: The same position. Step through the natural-looking move and what it allows.

line.say: The pawn attacks the knight. It also leaves c2 empty.
The knight lands on c2 with check and attacks the rook on a1. Taking it with the queen loses the queen to the bishop.
The king steps aside, and the knight takes the rook on a1 next.

claims.statement: The knight on c2 attacks the king's square e1 and the rook on a1.
At depth 16 the position after the king steps aside and the knight takes the rook is rated at least 3 pawns better for Black.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's knight attacks the queen. Step through the answer and look at what the knight is guarded by.

line.say: The queen moves with check and attacks the knight that attacked her.
Black blocks the check with the other knight. (Blocking with ...Nc6 fails too: the queen takes b7.)
The queen takes the knight, which nothing was guarding.

claims.statement: The queen on b5 attacks the knight on b4 and gives check along the diagonal to e8.
After Qb5+ the knight on b4 is loose (attacked, undefended).
At depth 16 the position after Qb5+ is rated at least 2.5 pawns better for White.
At depth 16 the position after Qb5+ Nc6 is rated at least 3 pawns better for White.

steps.text: **Before you attack a queen, look for a check.** An attacked queen is not forced to retreat: if she can give check and hit the attacker, the attacker must be guarded. In our online data, 43 of the 74 White players who reached this position found Qb5+ [V]. [I] The knight move is attractive because it attacks the queen and hits c2; the habit to build is to ask what the queen can do before asking where she goes.

steps.caption: Black to move. Step through a natural developing move and the reply, and count what attacks c7.

line.say: The knight develops and presses on d4, but it leaves c7 to the queen alone.
The knight attacks c7 and a7, and White's bishop on f4 already aims at c7. Two attackers against one defender.

claims.statement: After the developing move the bishop on f4 attacks c7.
After Nb5 two White pieces attack c7.
Only the queen defends c7.
At depth 16 the position after Nb5 is rated at least 1.5 pawns better for White.

steps.text: **The target is the pawn the bishop already eyes.** In this setup the bishop on f4 points at c7 from move two. Any second piece that can reach a square attacking c7 (the knight via b5) turns a pointer into a threat. Ask the question from both sides: which pawn do my pieces already attack, and what defends it? [I] This is why developing the knight to c6 can be a risk here: the pawn on c7 needs help.

steps.caption: Black to move. Step through the greedy line: the queen takes a pawn.

line.say: The queen attacks b2 and leaves d5 without a defender.
White develops with a threat on d5.
Black takes the pawn on b2, far from the king. White now has something stronger than recapturing.

claims.statement: After Nc3 the pawn on d5 is loose.
After the queen takes b2, nothing of White's attacks her yet.

steps.caption: White to move. The queen has taken b2 and attacks the rook on a1, but White does not recapture. Step through the knight capture.

line.say: The knight takes d5 and threatens Nc7+, a check that forks the king and the rook on a8. If Black takes the rook with Qxa1, White's queen takes her back.

claims.statement: The knight on d5 attacks c7 and e7.
The square c7 is empty, so a knight jump there would be a check.
At depth 16 the position after Nxd5 is rated at least 3 pawns better for White.
At depth 16 taking the rook with Qxa1 loses the queen to Qxa1: the position is at least 6 pawns better for White.

steps.caption: White to move. The knight on f3 is pinned to the queen. Step through a natural-looking developing move and Black's reply.

line.say: A normal developing move that eyes h7.
The pawn attacks the bishop on f4. Moving the knight would cost the queen. White will take on e5 and Black will retake with the f-pawn, which keeps attacking.

claims.statement: The bishop on g4 attacks the knight on f3.
After ...e5 the pawn attacks the bishop on f4.

steps.caption: White to move after the pawn recaptures on e5. The bishop must leave. Step through its retreat and Black's next pawn move.

line.say: The bishop steps away from the pawn.
The pawn forks the bishop on d3 and the pinned knight, which cannot move without losing the queen.

claims.statement: The pawn on e4 attacks both the bishop on d3 and the knight on f3.
At depth 16 the position after ...e4 is rated at least 2.5 pawns better for Black.

steps.caption: Black to move. A pawn on d4 looks free. Count the attackers and defenders, then step through.

line.say: The knight takes the pawn. Nothing of Black's defends the knight on its new square.
The queen takes the knight. Black has won a pawn and lost a piece.

claims.statement: Black has one attacker of d4 (the knight).
White has one defender of d4 (the queen).
After ...Nxd4 the knight on d4 is loose (attacked by the queen, defended by nothing).
At depth 16 the position after the queen takes is rated at least 2 pawns better for White.

steps.text: **Three questions before any capture or any developing move.** First, is anything of mine loose (attacked and unguarded), and is anything of theirs? Second, can I or they give a check that also attacks something? Third, which pieces are pinned, and which square would a pawn break attack? [I] These take seconds. Most boards in this lesson fell to one of them; the Nxd4 board also turned on piece values. The tests below include a calm position as well as traps.

steps.prompt: Teach it back. Imagine a beginner who plays the London System as White, or the Black side against it. In your own words, write four short answers.

fields.label: The idea: the questions to ask before a capture or a developing move
When a pinned or loose piece decides a position
One trap a beginner could set up on a board

steps.text: **Self-check.** Did you name the question (what is loose, what gives check, what is pinned)? Did you say when it matters (a piece with fewer guards than attackers)? Is your example a position a beginner could reach in a few moves? Did you name the tempting move that fails, and what answers it? If not, rewrite one answer. Nothing here is graded; the check is yours.

**Recap.** [1] Count attackers and defenders of the square a knight or bishop aims at. [2] A pawn move can empty a square for a forking knight. [3] An attacked queen may answer with a check. [4] A bishop eyeing a pawn plus a knight jump makes two attackers. [5] A pinned piece cannot defend; a pawn break can exploit it. [6] Equal counts do not mean a free pawn. [7] Checked: engine claims at depth 16, attacker counts and loose-piece sets.
